references.text: Jacob also blesses Pharaoh at the conclusion of their meeting (v.10), which frames the entire conversation with blessings.
Joseph introduces some of his brothers to Pharaoh, providing the immediate context for him then bringing his father Jacob before Pharaoh.

God's promise to Abraham that through his offspring all the families of the earth shall be blessed. Jacob's blessing of Pharaoh is part of the fulfillment of this promise—an descendant of Abraham brings blessing to the nations.

'Without doubt, the lesser is blessed by the greater.' This principle illuminates Jacob's blessing of Pharaoh: despite Pharaoh's political power, Jacob is the spiritually superior one who blesses him.
The psalm describes Israel's arrival in Egypt and God's blessing upon His people there, providing the broader context for Jacob's meeting with Pharaoh.
Jacob's role as a blesser expands from including Pharaoh to encompassing Joseph's sons, demonstrating the transfer of patriarchal blessing.
Acts 7:13 confirms the historical event in Genesis 47:7 where Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh.
God's blessing over Potiphar's house (39:5) is a precursor to the direct blessing Jacob gives Pharaoh (47:7), both mediated through Joseph's presence.
There is a theological progression from Jacob receiving blessing from God (35:9) to him exercising this authority toward Pharaoh (47:7).
The verses mark two distinct phases in Joseph's relationship with Pharaoh: interpreting dreams (41:26) and presenting his family (47:7).
A powerful contrast where Jacob moves from being a recipient of God's blessing (32:30) to exercising it toward Pharaoh (47:7).
The verses are connected as action (47:7) and theological explanation (48:15) of Jacob's authority to bless.
